{{Short description|In mathematics, when is n!+1 a square}}
{{distinguish|Brocard's conjecture}}
{{unsolved|mathematics|2=Does <math>n!+1=m^2</math> have integer solutions other than <math>n=4,5,7</math>?}}
'''Brocard's problem''' is a problem in [[mathematics]] that seeks [[integer]] values of <math>n</math> such that <math>n!+1</math> is a perfect square, where <math>n!</math> is the [[factorial]]. Only three values of <math>n</math> are known &mdash; 4, 5, 7 &mdash; and it is not known whether there are any more. Though research has extended far beyond n > 7, no additional solutions to the equation n! + 1 = m<sup>2</sup> are known.



More formally, it seeks pairs of integers <math>n</math> and <math>m</math> such that<math display="block">n!+1 = m^2.</math>The problem was posed by [[Henri Brocard]] in a pair of articles in 1876 and 1885,{{r|broc1|broc2}} and independently in 1913 by [[Srinivasa Ramanujan]].{{r|ramanujan}}

==Brown numbers==
Pairs of the numbers <math>(n,m)</math> that solve Brocard's problem were named '''Brown numbers''' by [[Clifford A. Pickover]] in his 1995 book ''Keys to Infinity'', after learning of the problem from Kevin S. Brown.{{r|pickover}} As of October 2022, there are only three known pairs of Brown numbers:
{{bi|left=1.6|(4,5), (5,11), and (7,71),}}
based on the equalities
{{bi|left=1.6|4! + 1 {{=}} 5<sup>2</sup> {{=}} 25,}}
{{bi|left=1.6|5! + 1 {{=}} 11<sup>2</sup> {{=}} 121, and}}
{{bi|left=1.6|7! + 1 {{=}} 71<sup>2</sup> {{=}} 5041.}}
[[Paul Erdős]] conjectured that no other solutions exist.{{r|erdos}} Computational searches have found no further solutions with <math>n \leq 10^{15}</math>.{{r|bergal|matson|epsgli}}

==Connection to the abc conjecture==
It would follow from the [[abc conjecture]] that there are only finitely many Brown numbers.{{r|overholt}}
More generally, it would also follow from the abc conjecture that
<math display=block>n!+A = k^2</math>
has only finitely many solutions, for any given integer <math>A</math>,{{r|dabrowski}} and that
<math display=block>n! = P(x)</math>
has only finitely many integer solutions, for any given polynomial <math>P(x)</math> of degree at least 2 with integer coefficients.{{r|luca}}
